title: The Map in the Attic
body:
Maya loved rainy Saturdays. She saw them as adventures. She climbed to her grandmother's attic to explore the dusty boxes lining the walls.

One Saturday in October, Maya noticed a box she had never opened. It was tucked behind old magazines and a broken umbrella stand. The box was made of tarnished brass with intricate designs.

Maya lifted the heavy lid. Inside was a folded, yellowed paper—a hand-drawn map of her grandmother's property. A large red X marked a spot near the old oak tree.

Maya rushed downstairs, clutching the map excitedly. "Grandma! Look what I found!" she called out.

Her grandmother studied the map and smiled knowingly. "Ah, you found it," she said softly. "I drew that map when I was about your age. I buried a time capsule there with my best friend, Eleanor. We promised to dig it up someday, but we never did."

Maya's eyes widened. "What's inside?"

"I don't entirely remember," her grandmother admitted with a laugh. "That was over fifty years ago. But I know we put in some photographs, a few coins, and a letter we wrote to our future selves."

The rain had stopped. Maya grabbed a small shovel excitedly and led her grandmother to the old oak tree. They dug at the red X. Soon, the shovel struck something solid. Maya revealed a rusted metal tin and pried it open. Inside were sepia-toned photographs of two young girls, a handful of old coins, and an envelope that read, "To whoever finds this—may your life be filled with as much joy as ours has been."

Maya looked at her grandmother, whose eyes glistened with happy tears. "Now it's your turn to make a time capsule," her grandmother whispered. Maya smiled. She already knew exactly what she would put inside.

title: How Honeybees Make Honey
body:
Have you ever wondered where honey comes from? It begins with the honeybee.

Honeybees live in large colonies inside hives. A single hive can contain up to 60,000 bees, and each bee has a specific job. The forager bee is the key worker for honey. Each day, they fly out to visit hundreds of flowers.

When a forager bee lands on a flower, it drinks a sugary liquid called nectar. The bee stores the nectar in a special pouch called the honey stomach. Unlike its regular stomach, the bee doesn't digest the nectar. Instead, it carries the nectar back to the hive.

Back at the hive, the forager bee passes the nectar to a house bee. The house bee chews the nectar for several minutes. This breaks down complex sugars into simpler ones, making it easier to preserve. Then, the house bee spreads the nectar into the walls of a honeycomb cell. Honeycomb cells, made of wax from the bees' own bodies, are shaped like perfect hexagons.

At first, the nectar is very watery. The bees fan the nectar with their wings to make the water evaporate. Once most of the water has evaporated, the nectar transforms into thick, sweet honey. Finally, the bees seal the cell with wax to keep the honey fresh.

Bees make more honey than needed. A strong hive can produce 50 to 100 pounds of honey in a single year. Beekeepers harvest extra honey by removing honeycomb frames from the hive. They use a machine called an extractor, which spins the honeycomb to release the honey. The honey is filtered and bottled.

Making honey is a team effort. A single tablespoon of honey represents the work of dozens of bees visiting thousands of flowers. The next time you taste honey, remember the journey it took.
